comment.value:
This paper presents a carefully constructed benchmark UVE-Bench for evaluating AI-generated videos (AIGVs) using multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as unified evaluators across 15 fine-grained quality aspects. The work offers a novel, rigorous, and comprehensive framework that significantly advances the evaluation methodology for video generation models.

Reviewers consistently recognize the benchmark’s novelty, thorough design, and high-quality human annotations, emphasizing its potential as a lasting platform for future research and fine-tuning of MLLM evaluators. However, they also raise concerns like limited temporal modeling capacity of current MLLMs, the omission of certain proprietary systems in the evaluation, and the scalability of pairwise human annotations. 

In the rebuttal and during the author-reviewers discussion, the authors have satisfactorily addressed these through detailed clarifications, inclusion of additional models, and discussion of future directions such as improved video encoding, dataset expansion with physically inconsistent videos, and few-shot adaptation methods.

Overall, the submission delivers a valuable contribution with actionable insights and a robust evaluation framework. The AC is happy to accept it. Congratulations!

Dear Area Chair and Reviewers,

We sincerely thank you for dedicating your valuable time to reviewing our paper and providing thoughtful feedback. We are encouraged by the positive comments from reviewers, especially regarding the `comprehensive, novel and rigorious design` of the benchmark (Reviewer ggWA, SN1J, iHvt), the `high quality` of the data (Reviewer SN1J, iHvt), `extensive evaluation` (Reviewer ggWA, SN1J, TPZx, iHvt), `insightful and actionable discussions` (Reviewer ggWA, SN1J, iHvt).

We are also grateful for the valuable suggestions, such as investigating negative instead of positive prompts (Reviewer iHvt), evaluating real videos in addition to AI-generated ones (Reviewer iHvt), conducting sensitivity analysis for thresholds $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (Reviewer iHvt, SN1J), discussing potential ways to further improve MLLMs' performance in AIGV evaluation (Reviewer ggWA, SN1J), evaluating more proprietary models (Reviewer SN1J) and considering fine-tuning MLLMs for this task as a future direction (Reviewer TPZx). We will incorporate relevant discussions and results, along with clarifications on other questions, in the next revision of our manuscript.

We are pleased that our rebuttal has addressed the concerns of Reviewers ggWA, SN1J, and iHvt, and that Reviewers TPZx and ggWA have decided to increase their ratings. We also appreciate Reviewer TPZx’s follow-up comments regarding (1) the value and long-term use of our benchmark, (2) ground-truth annotation and human baseline, and (3) insights from prompt design. We have provided detailed responses to each of these points in corresponding response to Reviewer TPZx.

Best,

UVE Authors

We sincerely thank you for the thoughtful further feedback and for acknowledging that our benchmark is `inherently valuable`. We also appreciate your willingness to raise your rating, and we would like to respond to the follow-up comments in more detail:

**1. On the Value and Future Use of the Benchmark**

We fully agree that fine-tuning MLLMs for AIGV evaluation is a promising and impactful direction. Importantly, we view this as complementary to — not in conflict with — the contributions of our current work. Our benchmark supports this future research in two key ways:
- **Evaluation Platform**: UVE-Bench can serve as a testbed to quantify improvements from fine-tuning efforts across models and configurations.
- **Ease of Integration**: Our UVE framework is designed to be model-agnostic. Fine-tuned models (with compatible architecture) can be easily integrated into UVE using a few lines of code:
```
from uve import UVE    
evaluator = UVE(model_name='xxx')    
evaluator.evaluate(video_path, aspect='xxx') 
```

**2. On Ground-truth Annotation and Human Baseline**
 
Indeed, human preference annotation of AIGVs may inevitably involve bias and subjectivity. To mitigate this, we take the following precautions:
- We design clear and detailed definitions for each aspect and corresponding evaluation criteria to reduce ambiguity.
- Annotators are instructed to only annotate video pairs for which they could confidently make a preference judgment.
- We report a Fleiss’ Kappa of 0.803, indicating strong inter-annotator agreement and suggesting minimal subjective variance. 

Regarding the "human baseline", we agree that this point could be better explained. Our intention is to introduce a reference point to better contextualize current MLLM performance in AIGV evaluation. We will revise the paper to clarify this.

**3. On Prompt Design Insights**

We acknowledge that findings such as “aspect-specific prompts help” or “more frames improve performance” may seem intuitive. However, we not only present them as general guidelines, but also translate them into concrete, actionable designs:
- We provide specific prompt templates for each evaluation aspect.
- We identify the suitable number of frames that balances performance with computational cost.

These can serve as effective default configurations in future work.

We hope that these clarifications help address your concerns. Thank you again for engaging deeply with our work!

Reviewer Follow-up Comments
Thank you for the responses, which partially address my concerns. I will increase my rating, although still have some follow-up comments:

1. On the Value and Future Use of the Benchmark
I agree with the authors that benchmarks also evolve over time. Constructing a new benchmark for AIGV evaluation — especially with fine-grained human annotations — is inherently valuable.

Given the rapid evolution of both MLLMs and VGMs, I believe the more impactful direction is to explore how to efficiently leverage such benchmark data, e.g., for fine-tuning open-source MLLMs to improve their robustness in VGM evaluation. In contrast, simply testing current MLLMs on the new dataset are bound to yield model-specific conclusions and may become obsolete as models evolve.  This limits the long-term utility and generalizability of these results.

2. On Ground-truth Annotation and Human Baseline
I would like to clarify that my concern is not about the participants of the human baseline, but rather that the authors themselves should not be involved in annotating the ground-truth labels, as their deep familiarity with the study design can unintentionally introduce bias.

Furthermore, the use of a separate “human baseline” is somewhat confusing. In video quality assessment, human annotations already serve as the ground truth. Introducing another set of human labels from three subjects merely reflects inter-subject variability, rather than providing a meaningful performance baseline. It would be helpful to clarify this distinction in the paper.

3. On Prompt Design Insights
Conclusions such as “aspect-specific prompts help” or “more frames improve performance” are highly intuitive and already widely known among MLLM users. As such, they may lack novelty and contribute limited methodological insight.

Dear Reviewer iHvt,

We are greatly encouraged by your recognition of our work and your insightful questions have helped us deepen our analysis. Please find our detailed responses below. We will also incorporate these discussions into the revised version of the paper.

>Q1: In Equation (1), what would happen if the calculation was done inversely using negative instead of positive? The paper currently focuses on positives—that is, MLLMs judging high-quality videos. I’m curious how the performance of various baseline models would change if there were criteria for evaluating low-quality videos.

This is an insightful angle we had not initially emphasized. In response, we revise the evaluation prompts to ask MLLMs whether a video is “bad” in a specific dimension, effectively inverting the original approach. Correspondingly, we also reverse the positive and negative token assignments in the computation of video ratings in Equation (1).
To illustrate the change, below are examples of the revised negative prompts alongside their original positive counterparts (for brevity, we show only the question part):
``` 
Dimension: Video-Text Alignment
Positive Prompt: Is the video content perfectly aligned with this text description: "${source}"?
Negative Prompt:  Is the video content not perfectly aligned with this text description: "${source}"?

Dimension: Dynamic Degree
Positive Prompt: Is the dynamic degree of the video content high? 
Negative Prompt: Is the dynamic degree of the video content low? 

Dimension: Static Quality
Positive Prompt: Is the visual quality of each individual frame good?
Negative Prompt: Is the visual quality of each individual frame bad?

Dimension: Temporal Quality
Positive Prompt: Is the visual quality of the video good from the temporal perspective?
Negative Prompt: Is the visual quality of the video bad from the temporal perspective?
``` 

We evaluate the Qwen2-VL-7B model using both positive and negative prompts across four dimensions. The results are shown in the table below:
| | Dynamic Degree | Static Quality | Temporal Quality | Video-Text Alignment | AVG |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Positive | 84.6 | 64.6 | 51.1 | 85.4 | 70.9 |
| Negative | 66.0 | 62.7 | 55.0 | 16.9 | 50.9 |

We observe that the performance varies notably across dimensions. For *Static Quality* and *Temporal Quality*, the difference between positive and negative prompts is relatively small. However, for *Dynamic Degree* and *Video-Text Alignment*, the performance with positive prompts is substantially higher.
Given these results, we recommend using positive prompts as the default setting.

>Q2: Are the thresholds α and β determined heuristically? Or is there a specific rationale or standard behind their selection?

Thanks for raising this important question. In the paper, we have chosen default values of $\alpha = 0.4$ and $\beta = 0.8$ to represent the thresholds for categorizing videos as "bad" and "good," respectively. However, we acknowledge the importance of conducting a sensitivity analysis.

To address this, we present the performance of four MLLMs across different values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$. As shown in the following tables, adjusting these thresholds reveals notable trends in performance:
1. Lowering $\beta$ (i.e., making the criteria for “good” more lenient) leads to increased agreement between MLLMs and humans in the "same good" category, resulting in higher performance.
2. Increasing $\alpha$ (i.e., making the criteria for “bad” stricter) also improves performance by enhancing alignment in the "same bad" category.

Despite the observed variations in performance as these parameters change, it is important to note that the relative performance of different MLLMs remains stable.

**$\alpha$=0.4**
| | $\beta$=0.7 | $\beta$=0.8 | $\beta$=0.9 |
|---|---|---|---|
| qwen2-vl-2b | 61.2 | 58.3 | 55.9 |
| longva | 64.1 | 61.6 | 57.6 |
| qwen2-vl-7b | 74.4 | 70.9 | 66.3 |
| qwen2-vl-72b | 77.3 | 75.4 | 72.5 |

**$\beta$=0.8**
| | $\alpha$=0.3 | $\alpha$=0.4 | $\alpha$=0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| qwen2-vl-2b | 56.7 | 58.3 | 62.8 |
| longva | 60.4 | 61.6 | 63.0 |
| qwen2-vl-7b | 69.6 | 70.9 | 72.5 |
| qwen2-vl-72b | 74.7 | 75.4 | 76.2 |

>Q3: What would happen if the method in the paper is applied for MLLMs to evaluate real videos (considering only single video rating)? If MLLMs were to assess both generated and real videos, would there be noticeable differences between generated and real video evaluations? This could provide valuable insights to readers.

Thank you for the thoughtful question—this is indeed an insightful point. To explore this idea, we conduct an additional experiment using 204 real videos from the TempCompass [1] dataset, which are sourced from the ShutterStock platform and features relatively good visual quality compared to average videos on YouTube. We applied the single video rating method described in our paper, using Qwen2-VL-7B to assess both Static Quality and Temporal Quality for these real videos. For comparison, we also report results of the videos generated by Open-Sora 1.2, CogVideoX-5B, HunyuanVideo, Movie Gen Video. 

As shown in the table below, real videos consistently receive higher scores than generated ones in both quality dimensions. Moreover, the relative rankings of the generative models closely align with our human perceptual judgments.
| | Static Quality | Temporal Quality |
|---|---|---|
| Open-Sora 1.2 | 63.2 | 59.7 |
| CogVideoX-5B | 70.0 | 67.3 |
| HunyuanVideo | 84.9 | 77.1 |
| Movie Gen Video | 84.3 | 74.7 |
| Real videos | 85.7 | 78.0 |
[1] TempCompass: Do Video LLMs Really Understand Videos?

>Q4: Recently, concerns about physical consistency in video generation have been raised. How does this work address such issues? Is this planned as future work? If future research can enable evaluation of physics through MLLMs, it would provide an excellent foundation for researchers going forward.

Thank you for highlighting this important topic! In fact, the *Motion Naturalness* dimension in our paper is related to physics commonsense in videos (the MLLM evaluators are prompted to check unnatual motions and object interactions that do not adhere to physical laws). According to our results, current MLLMs indeed struggle to evaluate this aspect. This task is challenging because it not only requires precise perception of temporal dynamics but also needs to associate it with conceptual knowledge of physical laws. To achieve this, future work could explore three directions:
- **Modeling**: Current MLLMs mostly sparsely sample frames and encode them independently using pre-trained vision encoder. This may lose some fine-grained temporal information. Therefore, a more effective video encoding technique that can extract denser temporal information is essential.
- **Data**: Current MLLMs' are mostly trained with real videos without sufficient exposure to videos contradicting physical laws during training. Therefore, the construction of a datasets of AIGVs that contradict physical laws (as well as corresponding annotations) could help.
- **Training Objective**: Most current MLLMs are only optimized with language loss. Therefore, they cannot fully understand the generative distribution within the visual domain, which is essential for physics understanding in videos. Therefore, future work can investigate integrating the visual generative loss into MLLM training.

Dear Reviewer TPZx,

Thank you for your comments! Our responses to your questions are below.

>Q1: Given N videos, we can easily construct ( \binom{N}{2} ) video paris, and pairwise preference data can be inferred directly from individual video ratings. Moreover, Section 4.6 supports the validity of converting single-video ratings into pairwise comparisons. As a result, the necessity of explicitly including a separate video pair comparison component becomes questionable.

This is an interesting question. We believe that investigating the direct video pair comparison capability of MLLMs is necessary for two reasons:
1. When an evaluator is presented with two videos simultaneously, it has direct access to comparative visual and temporal cues that may be missed when evaluating each video in isolation. This richer context often leads to more accurate judgments. As such, human evaluation protocols for AI-generated content frequently adopt direct pairwise or group-wise comparison methods [1,2], as they tend to produce more reliable and consistent preference annotations.
2. While single-to-pairwise adaptation proves to be an effective strategy for models with limited pairwise comparison ability, we have not yet seen conclusive evidence that this approach can universally replace direct pairwise comparison (e.g., the two methods are comparable in 72B-scale models). Therefore, the inclusion of direct video pair comparions ability remain important for MLLMs.

[1] Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback.

[2] ImageReward: Learning and Evaluating Human Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation.  

>Q2: Since both MLLMs and VGMs are continuously evolving, it may never be possible to draw principled conclusions that are universally applicable across all scenarios in this way, even though this work already covers relatively recent VGMs. Compared to evaluating the zero-shot performance of MLLMs for evaluating VGMs, exploring how to efficiently adapte them via few-shot learning or continual learning presents a more valuable research direction.

**Evolution of MLLMs**

Our primary goal is to investigate the ability of existing MLLMs in unified AIGV evaluation, a direction that is important while underexplored. Moreover, UVE-Bench, as proposed in our work, not only supports a systematic analysis of current MLLMs but also serves as a scalable platform that can continuously provide feedback for future model development. As such, the ongoing evolution of MLLMs does not diminish the relevance or value of UVE-Bench in advancing the field.

**Evolution of VGMs**

While new VGMs do introduce fresh challenges in AIGV evaluation, we humbly argue that it is unfair to consider this as a weakness because benchmarks themselves are also continuously evolving. Our UVE-Bench already incorporates most recent VGMs, which are sufficient to offer meaningful feedback for the development of AIGV evaluators in the immediate future.

**Few-shot or Continual Learning**    

We agree that few-shot learning of MLLMs in specific aspects AIGVs is valuable. However, since we focus on utilizing MLLMs as general-purpose AIGV evaluators, zero-shot performance remains a critical aspect — not only as a baseline but also as the foundation for any further fine-tuning. 

Moreover, it is important to clarify that our work is not constrained to the zero-shot setting. The proposed UVE framework is fully compatible with any continuouly fine-tuned MLLMs. The evaluation on UVE-Bench also involves MLLMs fine-tuned in particular aspects of AIGV evaluation, such as VideoScore-v1.1. 

>Q3: As stated in the paper, UVE-Bench is annotated by the authors themselves, which raises concerns about fairness. To ensure objectivity and statistical independence, the organizers of the subjective evaluation should refrain from participating, as their prior knowledge of the experimental setup can introduce unintended bias.

Thanks for raising this important point. In practice, the authors who annotate the ground-truth preference data do not participate in the subjective evaluation (i.e., human baseline), which ensures fairness.

>Q4: The observations presented in Sections 4.3 and 4.4 are relatively trivial. In the reviewer's view, the only meaningful takeaway is that the probability-based scoring strategy outperforms direct prompting of MLLMs for rating generation.

We respectfully disagree. Section 4.3 and 4.4 systematically explore various prompting and scoring strategies, which we believe are essential for identifying an effective configuration of the UVE framework, which highlights:
1. The utilization of positive/negative token probability for single video rating.
2. The adaptive use of yes/no and good/bad as the scoring tokens.
3. The advantage of detailed aspect-specific descriptions over simple binary questions, which better guide the MLLMs to focus on the evaluation aspect of interest. 

Following Reviewer iHvt's suggestion, we further conduct an additional experiment comparing positive versus negative formulations of the evaluation prompt (e.g., asking whether a video is bad rather than good). The results show that the original positive formulation yeilds better results (70.9% vs 50.9%). We believe these insights are non-trivial and would not have been obvious prior to conducting the experiments.

>Q1: MLLMs exhibit obvious performance gaps in temporal aspects (e.g., only 51-61% accuracy for motion naturalness in Table 5 vs. 88% human baseline), indicating inadequate understanding of fine-grained video dynamics despite high frame counts (Fig. 4, Sec 4.2). Thank you for raising this important point. We would like to address it from two perspectives:

**First**, we fully acknowledge that existing MLLMs face limitations in evaluating fine-grained temporal aspects of AIGVs. In fact, identifying and highlighting these gaps is a key motivation behind the development of UVE‑Bench. By providing a systematic evaluation of MLLMs' strengths and weaknesses in this context, our work aims to clarify: (1) the application scope of current MLLMs in AIGV evaluation and (2) future research directions.

**Second**, since our UVE framework is model-agnostic, it allows for easy integration of more advanced MLLMs as they become available. For example, when we incorporate the recently released Seed1.5‑VL (doubao-1.5-vision-pro-250328) as the backbone model, we observe improved performance in single video rating compared to the current state-of-the-art model, InterVL2.5‑MPO‑78B, as reported in our manuscript. This demonstrates the extensibility of our approach and its potential to keep pace with rapid developments in the MLLM landscape.
| | Overall Dynamic | Overall Static | Overall Temporal | Overall Alignment | AVG |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| InternVL2.5-MPO-78B | 84.3 | 72.8 | 61.5 | 87.4 | 78.2 |
| Seed1.5-VL | 83.2 | 82.4 | 70.5 | 84.2 | 80.0 |

>Q2: The reliance on pairwise human annotations, while reducing subjectivity (Sec 3.3), creates scalability limitations as annotating preferences across 15 aspects is labor-intensive compared to absolute ratings used in prior benchmarks (Sec 3.4-3.5).

This is an insightful observation. However, it's important to clarify that pairwise annotation does not necessarily entail higher annotation costs. In practice, the total number of pairwise comparisons can be flexibly controlled during dataset construction. For instance, given $N$ videos generated from the same prompt, it is not required to exhaustively annotate all $\binom{N}{2}$ possible pairs. Instead, a subset of $N$ pairs can be randomly sampled for annotation, which is equivalent to the cost of absolute rating.

>Q3: structural correctness evaluation remains weak (e.g., 60-67% asingle in Table 4) due to limited fine-grained visual perception (Sec 4.2). 

We appreciate your attention to this point. Indeed, current MLLMs exhibit limited ability to reliably assess structural correctness in AIGVs. Addressing this challenge requires not only improving the models’ ability to perceive fine-grained visual details, but also equipping them with a deeper conceptual understanding of object structure and physical plausibility. Looking ahead, we believe a promising direction involves curating AIGVs that exhibit typical structural errors. By incorporating these examples into the training of both vision encoders and MLLMs, we can help the models develop a more robust capability to distinguish between plausible and abnormal structures.

>Q4: Sparse frame sampling (Fig. 4) risks missing critical temporal details, but dense sampling is computationally costly—optimizing this trade-off requires further study (Sec 4.5).

Thank you for highlighting this important trade-off. To better understand the computational implications, we conduct an analysis of the inference time for Qwen2-VL-7B on the single video rating task, varying the number of frames per video. This evaluation is conducted on 80GB NVIDIA L20 GPU. As can be seen from the results below, the inference time does increase with the frame count per video. However, even with 16 frames per video, the total inference time across the entire UVE-Bench remains within 35 minutes, which we consider to be a practical and acceptable cost. This suggests that moderately dense sampling may be a feasible strategy without incurring prohibitive computational overhead.
| Frame Per Video | 1     | 2     | 4     | 8     | 16    |
|-----------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| Inference Time Per Video | 1.3s  | 2.0s  | 2.4s  | 2.9s  | 4.2s  |
| Total Inference Time (8 GPUs) | 10.6min | 16.4min | 19.9min | 24.8min | 35.0min |

>Q5: The single-to-pairwise adaptation helps smaller models but offers diminishing returns for larger ones (Fig. 5, Sec 4.6), suggesting the approach is not universally scalable.

We acknowledge this observation and agree that the benefits of single-to-pairwise adaptation tend to decrease with larger models. However, we would like to highlight its practical significance, particularly in resource-constrained scenarios. As demonstrated in Fig. 5 of our paper, Qwen2-VL-7B equipped with this adaptation performs comparably to the much larger Qwen2-VL-72B, while offering substantial savings in computational cost. In real-world applications, this strategy can be applied selectively—targeting models with limited pairwise comparison capacity.

>Q6: The current benchmark mainly focus on text-to-video tasks. Is is easy to transfer to other prevalent paradigms like image-to-video? 

Yes, our benchmark is readily extensible to image-to-video (I2V) generation. Most modern MLLMs already support interleaved image and video inputs, enabling straightforward adaptation. This can be achieved by tailoring the evaluation prompts to reflect I2V-specific dimensions, such as image-video alignment. Likewise, our benchmark construction pipeline can also be easily modified to support the assessment of MLLMs as I2V evaluators.

>Q7: Future work could explore efficient temporal modeling architectures and dynamic frame sampling to address temporal weaknesses, while expanding the benchmark to diverse generation tasks.

Thank you for the thoughtful suggestion! We agree that improved temporal modeling and frame sampling strategies are essential to understand the fine-grained temporal dynamics in videos. Expanding the benchmark to cover a broader range of generation tasks is also an excellent direction. We consider these promising avenues for future work and plan to investigate them further.

summary.value: In this paper, the authors explore evaluating ai-generated videos with the help of multi-modal large language models, which can serve as a unified evaluators across diverse quality aspects. Specifically, it introduces a zero-shot approach using pretrained MLLMs to evaluate 15 fine-grained dimensions, including static quality, temporal coherence, alignment, via tailored prompts for both single-video ratings and pairwise comparisons. In the experimental section, the proposed approach outperforms specialized evaluators but still lag behind human judgment, especially in temporally complex tasks. Some insights on optimal prompting, scoring strategies, and model scaling are provided to guide future research.

3) The extensive evaluation of ​16 MLLMs​ reveals their promising potential as unified evaluators (outperforming specialized tools like VBench/VideoScore, Tables 4–5), while identifying gaps in temporal understanding.

The weakness of this paper lies in the following aspects:
1) MLLMs exhibit obvious performance gaps in temporal aspects (e.g., only 51-61% accuracy for motion naturalness in Table 5 vs. 88% human baseline), indicating inadequate understanding of fine-grained video dynamics despite high frame counts (Fig. 4, Sec 4.2). This is also my major concerns: How strong is the ability and scope of MLLM to fully evaluate the various dimensions of the generated video?
2) The reliance on pairwise human annotations, while reducing subjectivity (Sec 3.3), creates scalability limitations as annotating preferences across 15 aspects is labor-intensive compared to absolute ratings used in prior benchmarks (Sec 3.4-3.5).

Future work could explore efficient temporal modeling architectures and dynamic frame sampling to address temporal weaknesses, while expanding the benchmark to diverse generation tasks.

summary.value:
The paper investigates whether  MLLMs can serve as unified evaluators for AI-generated videos, analogous to human assessment. Key contributions:

1. Unified Evaluation Framework: Proposes a zero-shot method to evaluate any AIGV aspect (e.g., motion naturalness, structural correctness) via MLLMs by simply modifying prompts, supporting both single-video rating (using token probabilities) and pairwise comparisons.

2. UVE-Bench: A novel benchmark with 4,042 human-annotated video pairs across 15 fine-grained aspects (grouped into Static Quality, Temporal Quality, Dynamic Degree, Video-Text Alignment). Features videos from 8 SOTA video generative models to challenge evaluators.

3. Comprehensive Analysis: Tests 16 MLLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Qwen2-VL-72B, InternVL2.5-78B), revealing that advanced MLLMs outperform specialized metrics (e.g., VBench) but still lag behind humans, especially in temporal dynamics.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This paper addresses the critical need for scalable, comprehensive AIGV evaluation as generative models advance. Unified MLLM-based evaluation eliminates costly per-aspect specialized training.

2. The benchmark is rigorous. 
- High-Quality Annotations: Pairwise preferences with Fleiss’ Kappa = 0.803 ensure reliability.
- Modern Video Sources: Uses outputs from 8 cutting-edge video generation model, exposing evaluators to realistic challenges.

3. The paper provides extensive empirical analysis and key insights obtained from the results:
- Tests 16 MLLMs across two evaluation modes, revealing that SOTA models (Qwen2-VL-72B, InternVL2.5-78B) outperform specialized tools (Table 4).
- Exposes MLLM-human gap (30+ points in pairwise accuracy) and temporal understanding weaknesses (Table 5).

4. It provides additional actionable Insights, which is important for following works to follow.
- Prompt Design: Detailed aspect-specific prompts boost performance (Fig. 2).
- Scoring Strategy: "Yes/no" tokens work best for scoring; direct score generation fails (Fig. 3).
- Efficiency: Larger models (72B+) better leverage increased frames for temporal tasks (Fig. 4).

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The study tests only one proprietary model (GPT-4o) vs. 15 open-source MLLMs, missing key industry benchmarks. Proprietary systems often lead in temporal reasoning (e.g., Gemini’s video processing). Omitting them understates the human-MLLM gap.

2. Thresholds α and β in Eq. 3 are manually set without sensitivity analysis. The authors could explore the parameter sensitivity.

3. The 30+ point accuracy gap (Table 5) is diagnosed but not addressed with concrete remedies. Are there any possible solutions for addressing the Human-MLLM Gap?

summary.value: This work studies the use of MLLMs for evaluating AIGVs, aiming for providing comprehensive and fine-grained evaluation for various aspects of AIGVs. Specifcially, a UVE-Bench is introduced, consisting of AIGVs generated by emerging video generative models. Pairwise human preference data across 15 aspects are collected. Through a comprehensive evaluation of existing MLLMs, this work concludes that the advanced MLLMs outperform specialized evaluation methods, although they still lag behind human evaluators. Insightful discussions about the design choices of MLLMs for AIGV evaluation are also provided.

strengths_contributions.value:
+ The introduced UVE-Bench provide human preference across fine-grained aspects.
+ Videos generated by both closed-source and open-source models are included, offering a comprehensive representation of state-of-the-art AIGC techniques.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Given N videos, we can easily construct  \( \binom{N}{2} \) video paris, and pairwise preference data can be inferred directly from individual video ratings. Moreover, Section 4.6 supports the validity of converting single-video ratings into pairwise comparisons. As a result, the necessity of explicitly including a separate video pair comparison component becomes questionable.

- Since both MLLMs and VGMs are continuously evolving, it may never be possible to draw principled conclusions that are universally applicable across all scenarios in this way, even though this work already covers relatively recent VGMs. Compared to evaluating the zero-shot performance of MLLMs for evaluating VGMs, exploring how to efficiently adapte them via few-shot learning or continual learning presents a more valuable research direction.

- As stated in the paper, UVE-Bench is annotated by the authors themselves, which raises concerns about fairness. To ensure objectivity and statistical independence, the organizers of the subjective evaluation should refrain from participating, as their prior knowledge of the experimental setup can introduce unintended bias.

- The observations presented in Sections 4.3 and 4.4 are relatively trivial. In the reviewer's view, the only meaningful takeaway is that the probability-based scoring strategy outperforms direct prompting of MLLMs for rating generation.

summary.value: This paper proposes the UVE benchmark and explores whether using MLLMs for evaluating video generation is appropriate. It also discusses the limitations of existing benchmarks and how the proposed method addresses them.

strengths_contributions.value:
I highly value this paper for the following reasons.

First, the paper clearly identifies the limitations and shortcomings of various benchmark datasets (e.g., AIGV-Assessor) and proposes solutions to address them. Specifically, it enhances evaluation by increasing the number of aspects considered and introduces new methods such as the Single Video Rating (Equation 1) and Video Pair Comparison (Equation 2).

Second, to increase the credibility of the UVE dataset, the authors provide a statistical evaluation of the dataset's quality in Section 3.4 using Fleiss' Kappa. This demonstrates that the dataset is of high quality. Moreover, Section 3.5 highlights the distinctions between the proposed dataset and previous ones.

Third, the paper compares the UVE benchmark with model-based evaluation metrics such as VBench and VideoScore, showcasing the strength and reliability of the proposed benchmark.

Lastly, the authors include a variety of experiments and evaluation methods that offer valuable insights for future MLLM evaluation strategies.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Here are a few questions rather than weaknesses:

1. In Equation (1), what would happen if the calculation was done inversely using negative instead of positive? The paper currently focuses on positives—that is, MLLMs judging high-quality videos. I’m curious how the performance of various baseline models would change if there were criteria for evaluating low-quality videos.

2. Are the thresholds α and β determined heuristically? Or is there a specific rationale or standard behind their selection?

3. What would happen if the method in the paper is applied for MLLMs to evaluate real videos (considering only single video rating)? If MLLMs were to assess both generated and real videos, would there be noticeable differences between generated and real video evaluations? This could provide valuable insights to readers.

4. Recently, concerns about physical consistency in video generation have been raised. How does this work address such issues? Is this planned as future work?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: As long as there are no licensing issues with the data generated by the model, there is no problem since the dataset was built directly.

dataset_code_comments.value: I checked the Hugging Face repository provided by the authors, and everything seems to be in order.

additional_feedback.value:
My feedback is as follows.

Recently, issues related to physics in generated videos have been raised, and papers such as “Do generative video models understand physical principles?” and “Generative Physical AI in Vision: A Survey” have emerged. title.value: UVE: Are MLLMs Unified Evaluators for AI-Generated Videos?

TLDR.value: This work investigates whether MLLMs can be used as unified evaluator for AI-generated videos and proposes a benchmark to assess this ability.

abstract.value: With the rapid growth of video generative models (VGMs), it is essential to develop reliable and comprehensive automatic metrics for AI-generated videos (AIGVs). Existing methods either use off-the-shelf models optimized for other tasks or rely on human assessment data to train specialized evaluators. These approaches are constrained to specific evaluation aspects and are difficult to scale with the increasing demands for finer-grained and more comprehensive evaluations. To address this issue, this work investigates the feasibility of using multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as a unified evaluator for AIGVs, leveraging their strong visual perception and language understanding capabilities. To evaluate the performance of automatic metrics in unified AIGV evaluation, we introduce a benchmark called UVE-Bench. UVE-Bench collects videos generated by state-of-the-art VGMs and provides pairwise human preference annotations across 15 evaluation aspects. Using UVE-Bench, we extensively evaluate 18 MLLMs. Our empirical results suggest that while advanced MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2VL-72B and InternVL2.5-78B) still lag behind human evaluators, they demonstrate promising ability in unified AIGV evaluation, significantly surpassing existing specialized evaluation methods. Additionally, we conduct an in-depth analysis of key design choices that impact the performance of MLLM-driven evaluators, offering valuable insights for future research on AIGV evaluation.

Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
